cards.explanation: The answer is the one who cares for the poor. The very first word of the psalm is "Blessed," and it lands on "…the one who cares for the poor…" (Psalm 41:1). David, Israel's king, doesn't start with a big title or a fancy résumé. He starts with somebody who looks out for people who have little.

The word is "deliver." David says the LORD "…will deliver him in the day of trouble." (Psalm 41:1). Trouble shows up for everybody, friends, but this person doesn't face it alone. That's good news on a hard day.

The answer is False. The text says the LORD will "…refuse to give him over to the will of his foes." (Psalm 41:2). He's protected, preserved and blessed, and he's not handed over. Enemies don't get the final word here.

The answer is that the LORD sustains and restores him. David says the LORD "…will sustain him on his bed of illness and restore him from his bed of sickness." (Psalm 41:3). Sustain and restore, those are the two things He does. I think that's a comfort to anybody who's ever been laid up.
The answer is heal him. David prays, "O LORD, be gracious to me; heal me…" (Psalm 41:4). He takes his sickness straight to the LORD. No hiding it, no fancy speech.
The answer is True, and that takes honesty. David prays, "heal me, for I have sinned against You." (Psalm 41:4). He doesn't dress it up. He just says it to the LORD.

The answer is "When will he die and be forgotten?" His enemies say it with malice (Psalm 41:5). They aren't just wishing him gone. They want his name gone too, and that's a cold thing to say about a man in a sickbed.

The word is slander. The visitor "…gathers slander in his heart; he goes out and spreads it abroad." (Psalm 41:6). He takes it out the door and passes it around. Some visitors should come with a receipt.

The answer is True, and it's a heavy one. They whisper that "A vile disease has been poured into him; he will never get up from where he lies!" (Psalm 41:8). Verse 7 says they "…imagine the worst for me…" I think that's hard to hear about yourself.

The answer is his close friend he trusted. David says, "Even my close friend whom I trusted, the one who shared my bread, has lifted up his heel against me." (Psalm 41:9). Enemies are one thing, friends. A friend from your own table hits different.

David asks the LORD to be gracious and raise him up. He prays, "But You, O LORD, be gracious to me and raise me up…" (Psalm 41:10). He turns to the LORD for it, which is where he went back in verse 4 too.

The answer is False. David's reason is this: "By this I know that You delight in me, for my enemy does not triumph over me." (Psalm 41:11). The text doesn't say the whispering stopped. It says the enemy doesn't triumph.

The answer is in His presence forever. David says, "…You uphold me and set me in Your presence forever." (Psalm 41:12). His enemies wanted him forgotten. Instead he's set right in front of the LORD, for good.

The answer is the LORD. The psalm closes with "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting. Amen and Amen." (Psalm 41:13). It started by blessing a person and ends by blessing the LORD. Nice bookends, friends.
